rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Science has disclosed little about this reality, and what it has disclosed deepens bewilderment; it will be unveiled in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: Science has very limited access and however much it has been able to unfold, has only increased man’s bewilderment

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After attention to the heavens, the discourse directs attention to the moon and sun as their great signs.
rows.anchor: directs his attention to the great signs they contain

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The moon’s light and sun’s lamp manifest God’s wisdom, universal providence, and power, and without them the world would remain dark.
rows.anchor: This also is a reference to God’s great wisdom and universal providence besides His power.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s signs of mercy and providence make a Day of accountability necessary; Islahi says this argument recurs throughout his exegesis.
rows.anchor: all the signs of God’s mercy and providence in this world necessitate a Day of accountability.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage turns from signs in the heavens to signs on earth, presenting humanity first as earth’s noblest creatures.
rows.anchor: attention is directed at the signs of the earth.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God grew humans from earth, returns them to it at death, and will bring them out of it again.
rows.anchor: the Almighty has grown them from the earth and later, to the earth He returns them and then He will bring them forth from it one day.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an’s eloquence makes the claim itself a clear proof: as vegetation grows, dies, and returns to earth, people do likewise; God’s revival of dead vegetation demonstrates His ability to resurrect people at will.
rows.anchor: just as vegetation sprouts from the earth, the Almighty has grown man from it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verbal nouns emphasize their respective verbs, but by different modes of emphasis that are difficult to render in translation.
rows.anchor: are meant to emphasize their respective verbs.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb can suggest growth with power and wisdom, ease, or elaboration; Islahi prefers elaborate creation joined with divine might and wisdom, supported by parallel verses and his discussion at 71:14.
rows.anchor: I have preferred the translation which reflects the elaborate manner in which man was created as well as the might and wisdom

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For the second verbal construction, Islahi prefers the sense of ease, while allowing other interpretations.
rows.anchor: I have preferred the meaning of ease for similar reasons; however, other interpretations are also possible.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The spread earth and its mountains are manifest signs of God’s power, wisdom, mercy, and favors; mountains stabilize the earth as a floor and make it balanced.
rows.anchor: the earth itself – a manifest sign which also attests to the great power and wisdom of the Almighty as well as to His infinite mercy and favours.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The stabilizing role of mountains is also stated in 16:15 and pictured as earth’s pegs in 78:6–7.
rows.anchor: He set firm mountains upon the earth lest it should move away with you

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God placed natural passes between mountains so people would not be trapped by them and could travel from place to place.
rows.anchor: he set them in a manner that man could go across these mountains through various naturally built passes between them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fijāj is the plural of fajj and means mountain passes, rather than ordinary paths; Islahi had explained it at 22:27.
rows.anchor: This word is not used for general paths; it is used for passes and paths between mountains.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the intervening verses, the discourse returns to Noah’s supplication; “Noah said, Lord” signals its resumption.
rows.anchor: have come to specify that Noah’s supplication is commencing.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Noah describes the final phase of his mission: after fully conveying the truth and leaving no excuse, his people defied him and followed affluent leaders whose wealth deepened their ruin.
rows.anchor: In this phase, Noah had communicated the truth to his people completely and they had been left with no excuse to deny it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi compares the people’s conceit to Quraysh in 68:14–15: wealthy and numerous, they dismissed warnings and earlier nations’ stories as ancient fables.
rows.anchor: since the Quraysh have abundant wealth and children, when they are asked to have fear of the evil fate they will meet

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kubbār is an intensive form of kabīr, describing the leaders’ very great schemes.
rows.anchor: is an exaggerated form of

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Noah’s opponents devised schemes to undermine his mission, alienate the masses from his call, and incite them against him; such tactics are familiar among arrogant leaders.
rows.anchor: they contrived great schemes to defeat the preaching mission of Noah (sws), to make the masses disgruntled by his calls and to incite them against him.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The leaders’ exhortation to keep the named idols explains their obduracy: the masses treated them as deities and were warned that any compromise endangered ancestral religion.
rows.anchor: They were regarded to be deities by their masses in every sense of the word.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The idols’ Arabic names and Noah’s people’s location north of Hijaz make it plausible that their language was Arabic.
rows.anchor: their language was Arabic.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Though the Flood erased Noah’s people, these idols were later worshipped by Arab tribes: Wadd by Banū Kalb, Suwā‘ by Hudhayl, Yaghūth by some Ṭay branches, Ya‘ūq by a Ḥamdān branch, and Nasr by a Ḥimyar branch.
rows.anchor: The tenacity of these idols is remarkable as the deluge had destroyed every sign of Noah’s people, yet these idols were still worshipped.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their sequence reflects descending rank: Wadd and Suwā‘ held higher status than Yaghūth, Ya‘ūq, and Nasr.
rows.anchor: The sequence in which these idols are mentioned here shows their ranks and status in descending order.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Noah grieves that the leaders led many astray and asks God to increase the wrongdoers’ error until they merit punishment and the earth is cleansed of them.
rows.anchor: Simultaneously, he prayed to the Almighty to increase these wrongdoers in further error so that they can swiftly become worthy of divine punishment

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Human beings were created to strive for success in life, not to burden the earth.
rows.anchor: The Almighty has not created man in this world to become a burden on it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage rejects the idea that God made humanity to be a burden on the earth.
rows.anchor: The Almighty has not created man in this world to become a burden on it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The drowning clause is a divine insertion into Noah’s prayer, like earlier insertions; its placement after the prayer’s first sentence signals that the prayer was timely and immediately accepted.
rows.anchor: They show that Noah (sws) had prayed at the right time and for the right purpose.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s wrath brings both punishments: the people drowned in this world and will be cast into Hellfire on Judgment Day.
rows.anchor: in this world they were drowned and on the Day of Judgement, they will be cast into the fire of Hell.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although the people relied on worldly power and alleged deities when warned, none will help them when God’s punishment arrives.
rows.anchor: when the punishment of God would come, they will find no one to help them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the divine insertion, Noah’s prayer resumes; repeating “Noah said, Lord” makes the resumption clear, since without the insertion the repetition would be unnecessary.
rows.anchor: After the insertion verses, the prayer of Noah (sws) resumes from this verse.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Arabic negation mā can mean that no one is in the house; the prayer’s sweeping negation follows from the reasons already given.
rows.anchor: it would mean that there is no one in the house.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A messenger determines his people’s fate in this world after conveying the truth fully and leaving them no excuse; they then merit punishment.
rows.anchor: A rasūl decides the fate of his nation in this world because he communicates the truth to his people

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Noah had found no trace of faith or piety in his people and judged that any spared would produce only disbelievers and sinners.
rows.anchor: Noah (sws) had fully evaluated his people and seen that not the slightest trace of piety and faith remained in them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although each child is born with God-given true nature, parents, surroundings, and society shape the child’s education; good surroundings support faith, while unbelieving surroundings form the child accordingly.
rows.anchor: his parents, his environment and the society play the greatest role in his instruction and training.

rows.speaker: the Prophet (sws)
rows.claim: Abū Hurayrah reports from the Prophet that every child is born on true nature and parents make the child a Jew, Christian, or Magian; Islahi cites al-Bukhārī, vol. 1, p. 456, no. 1293.
rows.anchor: narrative reported by Abū Hurayrah (rta) from the Prophet (sws)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Noah asks forgiveness for himself, his parents, believers who enter his home, and all believing men and women, then asks ruin for obstinate polytheists and disbelievers.
rows.anchor: Here, at the end, Noah (sws) has sought forgiveness for himself,

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Noah’s prayer reflects the parents’ great right upon their children; the Qur’an emphasizes this in several places.
rows.anchor: It is evident from Noah’s seeking forgiveness for his parents that the parents have a great right on their children

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an does not indicate whether Noah’s parents were believers; they may have died before or during his mission, and praying for them fulfilled their right without divine prohibition.
rows.anchor: Some people are of the opinion that his parents were believers;

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording implies that in his final phase Noah announced that anyone seeking refuge from punishment should take shelter in his house.
rows.anchor: in the last phase Noah (sws) had announced among his people that those who want to seek refuge from the punishment should seek shelter in his house.

none: Colophon and closing date only; no commentary point.
